title: #69 Don't Let Students Copy the Questions in the Do Now
author: Barton, Craig
summary: Building on his earlier tip about not displaying the title and date during a Do Now, Barton extends the same logic to a further habit: students copying down the Do Now questions themselves before answering them. He argues copying is a cognitively passive activity that looks productive to a teacher circulating or glancing from the front, and that it sets students up for a further round of passive copying when answers are reviewed, producing a tidy exercise book that earns praise despite representing very little actual thinking. He pre-empts the standard teacher objection -- that students need the questions copied down for later revision -- by pointing out that in his experience, essentially no student actually revises from Do Now answers. His conclusion groups this with the earlier title-and-date tip under a single principle: strip out every low-value copying task from the start of the lesson so students begin thinking, rather than transcribing, from minute one.
points: Copying down Do Now questions is cognitively passive but visually indistinguishable from real work to a teacher circulating or observing from the front, making it an easy habit to miss.
The pattern compounds: students primed to copy questions are also primed to copy answers later, producing a book that looks thorough while representing little genuine thinking.
Barton directly rebuts the "students need it for revision" justification with a pointed empirical challenge: he has never seen a student actually revise from Do Now answers.

This tip explicitly links to his earlier title-and-date tip, framing both as instances of the same underlying principle -- remove low-value copying tasks to protect the first minutes of a lesson for real thinking.
quotes: A follow-on from that tip is to tell students not to copy down the questions from the Do Now.

Students love nothing more than copying things down. It is a cognitively passive activity that, from the teacher’s view at the front of the class - or even from a quick glance during circulation - gives the impression that they are busy beavering away.

Better still, students are primed to copy the answers down when the teacher goes through them, even adding the flourish of a few ticks and crosses, resulting in a beautiful exercise book that will no doubt be lavished with praise when it is checked.

The argument teachers often give when I suggest stopping students from copying down the question is that the answers to the Do Now will make no sense to students when they come to revise. My response: show me one student who has ever used the Do Now to revise.
We want to remove as many barriers as possible to students thinking and learning from the very first minute of each of our lessons.
